By December 2014, South Sudan had become a cautionary tale of post-colonial state fragility. I didn't plan to abandon the FSO Safer in 2015. When Yemen's civil war erupted, we had no choice—the conflict made it impossible to maintain operations. The tanker, already aging at 47 years old, became a ghost ship anchored five miles off the coast, holding a million barrels of crude worth $80 million.

For eight years, we watched helplessly as our vessel decayed in the Red Sea. The pressure mounted. Environmental experts warned it was a "ticking time bomb"—the oil could explode, the hull could collapse, unleashing a catastrophe four times worse than the Exxon Valdez disaster. A spill would devastate 200,000 jobs, poison drinking water for 10 million people, and destroy Yemen's fisheries entirely.

When the UN finally launched the $141 million removal operation in August 2023, pumping 4,000 barrels per hour onto the replacement vessel Nautica, I felt relief mixed with guilt. We'd created an environmental sword hanging over millions of innocent people. Now, at least, someone was trying to defuse it.

Y 2023-11, A Historical Record of Crisis and Despair in Venezuela As a historian documenting the early twenty-first century, I observe Venezuela's humanitarian collapse through the lens of human tragedy. Between 2015 and 2022, suicide rates nearly doubled—from 3.8 to 9.3 per 100,000 inhabitants—a stark demographic shift reflecting deeper structural collapse. The case of Ernesto, a fifty-year-old former salesman, exemplifies this pattern. Once a breadwinner and community contributor, he succumbed to untreated illness and economic devastation, leaving a final note: "I will not continue being dead in life." His death was not isolated but symptomatic of systemic failure. Venezuela's eight-year recession (2013-2021) eroded GDP by four-fifths, triggering hyperinflation, currency collapse, and mass migration of seven million citizens. The humanitarian emergency—characterized by deteriorated economic, institutional, and social structures—created conditions where despair became epidemic. Historians note that vulnerable populations bore the heaviest burden: men aged 40-50 facing unemployment, young people aged 15-24 struggling with anxiety and depression, and families fractured by migration. Psychologists documented that as macro-economic conditions deteriorated, so did access to food, medicine, and mental health services. By 2023, this crisis represented not merely statistical increase but a historical watershed—evidence of state failure and collective trauma reshaping Venezuelan society.

I was no longer just a resident; I was a witness to the end of an era.

I was a survivor of Japan's lost decades, and now I had to survive this transformation too, hoping their gamble would secure my final years.

While the mayor celebrates the "excellent result" of our city’s output being sold to 54 countries, I am left in the silence of a town that has been hollowed out to feed a global market. They are building their balance sheets on the back of our exhaustion. We are the engine of this prosperity, yet we are the ones left behind in the dust of the departing cargo, watching our city’s lifeblood vanish into the horizon for the sake of a surplus we will never see.

Y [2017-06], I sit on the dusty floor of a classroom in Aden, squeezed between 170 other children. The air is thick with heat and the fear of the cholera outbreak that has already shuttered schools in our neighborhood. My hands are empty; there are no books. The ones we were supposed to have were stolen, their pages torn or rewritten by insurgents to erase our history and replace it with their own lies. My teacher looks exhausted, his eyes reflecting the fifteen years of progress he watched crumble in a single year. He tells us that the eighty million dollars meant for our future—money from the world—was snatched away by those who hold the telecommunications lines hostage. We are trapped in a cycle of displacement, fleeing the violence in Taiz only to find ourselves in overcrowded rooms where even the simple act of learning feels like an act of defiance. Tomorrow, the exam results will be posted on a website, not sent to Sana’a, because we cannot trust them not to tamper with our futures. I stare at the blank wall, wondering if I will ever hold a real book again, or if my education will remain a casualty of this endless, bitter war.
